Every number here is claimed against math_objects.json; run check_outline.py after any change.
title: The Secret Code of the MINIMOG

scenes._comment: Series main title, then this episode's subtitle; see titles/outline.json.
scenes.subtitle: sub.ep3

scenes.title: Twelve cells
scenes.summary: Ada keeps her promise not to memorize: she sends the twelve cards into Conway's 3 x 4 MINIMOG, where every card always sits in the same cell, and numbers its rows 0, 1, 2.

beats.purpose: Ada's better way: the twelve cards fly into Conway's MINIMOG, every card in its own cell
beats.gist: PASCAL: You said there's a better way than memorizing. ADA: There is. Watch. (The cards fly into the grid.) Twelve cards, three rows, four columns: Conway's MINIMOG. Every card always sits in the same cell. PASCAL: Mini what? ADA: A small version of Curtis's MOG, the Miracle Octad Generator. PASCAL: Bless you.

beats.purpose: The rows are numbered 0, 1, 2 from the top, numbers that live on a clock
beats.gist: ADA: Number the rows zero, one, two. PASCAL: Why not one, two, three? ADA: Because these three go round a clock.

scenes.title: A three-hour clock
scenes.summary: Arithmetic mod 3 on a clock with three hours: 2 + 1 = 0 and 2 + 2 = 1. Sophie recognizes it in the kitten's wrapped diagonal, where row plus column is always 0 mod 3.

beats.purpose: A clock with three hours: its hand moves as the sums are said; this is arithmetic mod 3
beats.gist: ADA: A clock with three hours (the hand sweeps 0, 1, 2). Two plus one goes round to zero (it ticks on to 0). EULER: Like my clock, only smaller. ADA: Two plus two is one (two ticks from 2). That's arithmetic mod three.

beats.purpose: Sophie recognizes the clock in Episode 2's wrapped diagonal: row plus column is 0 mod 3 on it
beats.gist: SOPHIE: I've seen that clock: the kitten's diagonal that ran off the edge and came back. ADA: Along it, row plus column is always zero, mod three. SOPHIE: The wrap was the clock all along.

scenes.title: Nine words
scenes.summary: Pick a and b on the clock; the codeword is (b, a, a+b, a+2b), and each place is a coordinate. Viewers build the one for a = b = 1: 1, 1, 2, 0. Three choices each give nine words, the tetracode. Any two coordinates pin down the whole word, checked for all six pairs of places: Ada's favorite property.

beats.purpose: A codeword: four numbers b, a, a+b, a+2b on the three-hour clock; each place is a coordinate
beats.gist: ADA: Pick two hours, a and b. Write b, then a, then a plus b, then a plus two b, round the clock. That's a codeword; each place is a coordinate.

beats.purpose: Viewers build the word for a = b = 1; a + 2b = 3 goes round to 0
beats.gist: ADA: Take a equals one and b equals one. (Pause.) b is one, a is one, a plus b is two, a plus two b is three, which goes round to zero. SOPHIE: One, one, two, zero.

beats.purpose: Three choices for a and three for b: nine codewords, the tetracode
beats.gist: ADA: Three choices for a, three for b: nine codewords, the tetracode. PASCAL: Even I could memorize nine. ADA: You won't have to.

beats.purpose: Any two coordinates determine the word: shown for the first two, checked for all six pairs of places
establishes: Any two coordinates determine a tetracode word
beats.gist: ADA: My favorite part: any two coordinates pin down the whole word. SOPHIE: Any two? ADA: The first two say one and one: only one, one, two, zero starts that way. Six ways to pick two places; I checked all six.

scenes.title: Odd man out
scenes.summary: Mark six cards in the grid and read each column. One card: its row. Two cards: the row left out, the odd man out. Empty or full: a wildcard that fits any row. The readings must spell a tetracode word, and then the hand is a hexad. Column counts 0, 1, 2, 3 always fail: only two columns give a row, and any two coordinates fit a word, so the words alone would pass all 216 such hands, and none is a hexad.

beats.purpose: The test begins: mark six cards and read each column; a column with one card gives its row
beats.gist: ADA: Mark six cards and read each column. One card? Read its row. Five is in row one.

beats.purpose: Two cards in a column give the row left out: the odd man out
beats.gist: ADA: Two cards? Read the row they leave out. Six and four leave out row one: the odd man out. PASCAL: Poor five.

beats.purpose: An empty or full column is a wildcard, which fits any row
beats.gist: ADA: An empty column, or a full one, is a wildcard. It fits any row.

beats.purpose: The rule: the four readings must spell a codeword, a wildcard fitting anything; passing means a hexad
beats.gist: ADA: The rows you read must spell one of the nine codewords; a wildcard fits anything. Pass, and the hand is a hexad.

beats.purpose: Column counts 0, 1, 2, 3 always fail: two readings always fit a word, and none of these hands is a hexad
beats.gist: ADA: One exception: columns holding zero, one, two and three cards fail. PASCAL: Why? ADA: Only two columns give a row, and any two fit a word, so the words would pass every such hand, and none is a hexad. PASCAL: A patch. ADA: A necessary one.

scenes.title: Test the hands
scenes.summary: The opening hand from Episode 1 reads 1, 1, 2, 2; its first two coordinates force 1, 1, 2, 0, the word from the clock; the last disagrees, so it is not a hexad. The hand 1 to 6 is all wildcards: a hexad. The 24-hand Ada left Pascal fits 1, 1, 2, 0 too, but its counts are forbidden. Euler: three hands are not a proof; the paper runs the test on all 924 hands.

beats.purpose: Episode 1's opening hand in the grid: column counts 2, 1, 2, 1 and readings 1, 1, 2, 2
beats.gist: ADA: The hand our first game started with: zero, two, four, six, seven, eleven. The columns read one, one, two, two. (Pause: does it spell a codeword?)

beats.purpose: The first two readings force 1, 1, 2, 0; the last disagrees, so the hand is not a hexad
beats.gist: ADA: The first two are one and one: that pins down one, one, two, zero. The third agrees; the last says two, the word says zero. EULER: Could another word fit? ADA: No: two coordinates pin down the word, so there is only one to try. Not a hexad. EULER: The hand we started with wasn't special.

beats.purpose: The hand 1 to 6: two full and two empty columns, all wildcards, so a hexad
beats.gist: ADA: One to six: two full columns, two empty. Four wildcards: it fits every word, a hexad. EULER: Sophie's dead hand, at a glance.

beats.purpose: The 24-hand Ada left Pascal fits 1, 1, 2, 0, but its counts 3, 1, 2, 0 are forbidden
beats.gist: ADA: The twenty-four I left Pascal in our first game. Its rows fit one, one, two, zero, but its columns hold three, one, two and zero cards. Forbidden. PASCAL: I knew I liked that hand.

beats.purpose: Three examples are not a proof; the paper runs the test on all 924 hands and it picks out exactly the hexads
beats.gist: EULER: Three hands aren't a proof. ADA: No. The paper runs the test on all nine hundred twenty-four hands, and it picks out exactly the hexads. EULER: That will do.

scenes.title: Repair
scenes.summary: The forced word wants a 0 in the last column, so 11 out, 9 in repairs the opening hand. Of its 36 single swaps, six repair it: three up (0 for 1, 2 for 10, 6 for 8), which the game forbids, and three down (4 for 3, 7 for 5, 11 for 9). PASCAL: Seven for five. That was my move! It passes the test, fitting 2, 1, 0, 2. Skill, or one of three repairs among fourteen moves?

beats.purpose: The word wants a 0 in the last column: moving its card from row 2 to row 0, 11 out and 9 in, makes a hexad
beats.gist: PASCAL: My hand failed. Can you fix it? ADA: One swap. The word wants a zero in the last column: eleven out, nine in. Now it reads one, one, two, zero: a hexad.

beats.purpose: 36 single swaps, six repairs: three up, which the game forbids, and three down
establishes: Exactly six single swaps turn the opening hand into a hexad
beats.gist: ADA: Six out, six in: thirty-six swaps, six make a hexad. Each is a repair. Three go up: zero for one, two for ten, six for eight. PASCAL: Up isn't allowed! ADA: Not in the game. Three go down: four for three, seven for five, eleven for nine.

beats.purpose: Seven for five was Pascal's opening move: a repair, fitting the word 2, 1, 0, 2
beats.gist: PASCAL: Seven for five. That was my move! ADA: And it passes: the new hand fits two, one, zero, two. PASCAL: Skill. Obviously. ADA: Or luck. Three of your fourteen moves were repairs.

scenes.title: Signed patterns
scenes.summary: A brief look at signed patterns and the ternary Golay code behind the test. Cut if the episode runs long.

scenes.title: Why does it work?
scenes.summary: EULER: Repair the hand, then win. Every time. I want to know why. PASCAL: Who cares why? It works.

beats.purpose: Euler notices that whoever repaired the hand won every game so far, and wants to know why
beats.gist: EULER: Every game we've played, whoever repaired the hand went on to win. I want to know why. PASCAL: Who cares why? It works. ADA: I care.
